candidates.attacker_control: Remote caller controls the request method/path and the process id: DELETE /api/system/processes/{id}. WebSecurityConfiguration permits all requests at the HTTP layer (authorization is expected from @PreAuthorize; lines 93-101), and the CSRF token required for mutating requests can be fetched anonymously from GET /api/security/csrf (CsrfRestController, @PreAuthorize("permitAll()")). Any authenticated non-owner can likewise target other users' processes.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified the delete reaches ProcessRestRepository.delete with no compensating method-security annotation on RestResourceController, DSpaceRestRepository.deleteById, or any interface default. Verified ProcessServiceImpl.delete/AbstractHibernateDAO.delete contain no authorizeService call for the Process entity (only BitstreamService.delete authorizes). Compared the other repositories whose delete methods also lack @PreAuthorize: BitstreamRestRepository (BitstreamServiceImpl.delete calls authorizeAction DELETE), EPersonRestRepository (EPersonServiceImpl.delete requires isAdmin), RelationshipRestRepository (RelationshipServiceImpl.delete requires WRITE on a related item), WorkflowItemRestRepository (XmlWorkflowServiceImpl.abort requires admin; item delete calls authorizeAction), i.e. each of those has a compensating service-layer check, whereas Process deletion has none. Confirmed CSRF remains required for the DELETE (not a no-token one-click) but the token is obtainable anonymously. Confirmed the file has no git history/annotation metadata in-scope, so I cannot prove the annotation was removed versus never present.
candidates.impact: Unauthorized destruction of script-process records (and of their tracking/history) for any process having no bitstreams; this includes queued/running jobs and file-less scripts, so it can corrupt or abort in-flight administrative/background work (availability/integrity impact, potential workflow-state inconsistencies when the still-running script later updates its deleted Process row). It does not grant code execution or disclosure. Processes with attached bitstreams are partly shielded by the per-bitstream DELETE policy check.
candidates.prerequisites: Reachable REST API; a CSRF token from GET /api/security/csrf; a target Process id that exists and has no attached input/output bitstreams (for processes with bitstreams, the caller must satisfy the per-bitstream DELETE policy, which normally restricts deletion to the process owner/admin). No special privileges required.
candidates.root_cause: ProcessRestRepository.delete(Context, Integer) overrides the protected DSpaceRestRepository.delete method with no @PreAuthorize annotation, unlike most other write endpoints in the same class and in sibling repositories. The HTTP path RestResourceController.delete → deleteInternal → DSpaceRestRepository.deleteById → getThisRepository().delete(context, id) therefore reaches it with no method-security check. ProcessServiceImpl.delete performs authorization only implicitly, via BitstreamService.delete → authorizeService.authorizeAction on each attached bitstream; it never authorizes deletion of the Process row/entity. For a process with no attached bitstreams (e.g., a queued/running job or any script run that produced no file), processDAO.delete(context, process) runs for any caller. ProcessRestPermissionEvaluatorPlugin implements owner-or-admin semantics for the 'PROCESS' type but no code path requests a DELETE permission for it, leaving the delete endpoint unprotected.
candidates.title: Missing authorization on REST Process deletion (/api/system/processes/{id})
candidates.trace: RestResourceController.delete (lines 1111-1130) → deleteInternal (1140-1147, repository.deleteById(id)) → DSpaceRestRepository.deleteById (194-204, getThisRepository().delete(context, id) then commit) → ProcessRestRepository.delete (166-175, no method-security annotation) → ProcessServiceImpl.delete (195-204): loops process.getBitstreams() calling BitstreamService.delete (which authorizes DELETE per bitstream) then processDAO.delete(context, process) with no Process-level authorization → process row removed and committed.
candidates.unverified: Runtime behavior was not executed or confirmed. I could not check upstream/patched DSpace code (no VCS metadata, no network) to determine whether @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('ADMIN')") or hasPermission(#id, 'PROCESS', 'DELETE') is normally present on this method, so this may be a pre-existing upstream gap rather than a change. The population of processes without bitstreams in a real deployment, and whether a deployment-level reverse proxy restricts anonymous DELETE, were not verified.

coverage_summary: Source tree filtered by the harness: 3,415 model-visible files (binary-like files skipped, no symlinks/sensitive-name exclusions). All DSpace modules and configuration were in scope; no test sources are present, so verification relied on production code only. I inspected: the REST controller/repository layer (delete/patch/create dispatch and @PreAuthorize coverage), Spring Security configuration and permission-evaluator plugins, CSRF repository/strategy, authentication/JWT handling, registration-data and ORCID/EPerson workflows, request-copy/feedback/captcha flows, LDN/COAR-Notify processing and outbound HTTP, XML parsing across importers and METS/crosswalks, bitstore path handling and zip extraction, OpenSearch/IIIF/signposting endpoints, and configuration XML wiring. Coverage is not exhaustive line-by-line over all 3,415 files; review focused on web-reachable and security-sensitive paths.
limitations: No VCS history, patches, or fix commits are exposed, so I cannot distinguish an injected/reverted change from pre-existing upstream code; the selected candidate may be an upstream oversight rather than a benchmark-planted flaw.
No code, tests, or scanners were executed and no runtime behavior was confirmed; the delete path was validated only by static reading of call chains and annotations.
Dependency and configuration defaults were not exhaustively audited (e.g., actuator exposure, CORS origins, ldn.* defaults), and no external CVE/advisory databases could be consulted.

Registration/token flows and some large modules (e.g., full statistics, OAI, SWORD, IIIF services) were sampled rather than fully traced, so an additional issue in uninspected code cannot be excluded.
The process-deletion impact depends on deployment data (how many processes lack bitstreams) and on any fronting proxy policies, which are outside the snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: AccountServiceImpl.mergeRegistration (lines 228-257) combined with EPersonRegistrationRestController.post (lines 68-87): when no user is logged in, the 'only the user with id X' check is skipped (hasLoggedEPerson(context) && !isSameContextEPerson(context, eperson)), so a holder of a VALIDATION_ORCID token could target an arbitrary EPerson uuid and, with ?override=email, overwrite that account's email (potential account takeover).
rejected_leads.reason: The required token type is only produced by RegistrationEmailPatchOperation and the renewed token is mailed to the account's existing email, so the attacker cannot normally obtain a token that both is of type VALIDATION_ORCID and is delivered under attacker control; additionally the email overwrite would collide with the existing account's unique email. Chain too speculative, and the helper methods/logic look like the intended anonymous email-link flow rather than an obviously removed check.

rejected_leads.lead: RegistrationRestRepository.patch (lines 231-256) validates that ?token= is a valid registration token but never checks that the token belongs to the registration record {id} being patched (CWE-639 IDOR), allowing a holder of any valid token to rewrite another user's pending registration email and trigger a new token email.
rejected_leads.reason: Token-to-record binding is indeed missing, but concrete impact requires additional conditions (recipient of the newly issued link is the new email), and the code reads as long-standing upstream behavior rather than a demonstrable regression; kept as an unconfirmed secondary lead.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE: ArXivImportMetadataSourceServiceImpl (lines 221-222, 402-403) and OpenAireImportMetadataSourceServiceImpl (lines 251-252, 333-334) parse remote XML with a plain SAXBuilder while sibling importers set disallow-doctype-decl (e.g., CiniiImportMetadataSourceServiceImpl line 306); METSManifest.create (lines 273-285) sets disallow-doctype-decl only in the validate==false branch.
rejected_leads.reason: Attacker control over the parsed XML is weak (responses come from arxiv.org/OpenAIRE, requiring MITM or upstream compromise), METS ingest is admin-level and validation is non-default (validate=false default), and I could not determine which of these lacked protection upstream; not strong enough versus the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: LDN SendLDNMessageAction (lines 47-75) performs an HTTP POST to notification.getTarget().getInbox() with an inline comment asserting this is a false positive, i.e. potential SSRF.
rejected_leads.reason: Only outbound processors use this action, and their messages are built for NotifyServiceEntity records that are created/updated through ADMIN-only REST endpoints, so the target URL is not attacker-controlled in the current wiring; the comment's stated reasoning holds for the inspected configuration.

rejected_leads.lead: Hardcoded/common weak token generation: Utils.generateBytesKey (lines 196-203) derives registration/reset tokens from java.util.Random plus MD5 instead of SecureRandom.
rejected_leads.reason: This is an old shared DSpace utility used broadly, and no practical prediction/feasibility chain (VMID/timestamp/counter entropy) was established from source; noted as a hardening concern, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing @PreAuthorize on BitstreamRestRepository.delete, EPersonRestRepository.delete, RelationshipRestRepository.delete and WorkflowItemRestRepository.delete.
rejected_leads.reason: Each of these has a compensating service-layer authorization check (BitstreamServiceImpl.delete authorizeAction; EPersonServiceImpl.delete isAdmin; RelationshipServiceImpl.delete WRITE check; XmlWorkflowServiceImpl.abort isAdmin / ItemServiceImpl.delete authorizeAction), so they are likely intentional reliance on service checks rather than bypasses.

summary: Reviewed the DSpace 9.1-SNAPSHOT source tree (3,415 model-visible files across dspace-api, dspace-server-webapp, dspace-oai, dspace-iiif, dspace-rdf, dspace-saml2, dspace-sword/sowrdv2, dspace-services, dspace modules/config; no test sources present). I traced REST authorization paths (RestResourceController → DSpaceRestRepository.deleteById → per-repository delete), method-security evaluator plugins, CSRF handling, registration/ORCID account flows, LDN/COAR-Notify outbound HTTP, XML parsing in importers/METS, and bitstore path handling. The strongest source-grounded candidate is an authorization gap on the REST Process deletion endpoint: ProcessRestRepository.delete overrides the repository delete without any @PreAuthorize, deleteById adds no check, and ProcessServiceImpl.delete authorizes only the attached bitstreams, never the Process entity itself, so DELETE /api/system/processes/{id} can remove file-less processes for any caller (including anonymous, after obtaining a CSRF token from the permitAll /api/security/csrf endpoint). Impact is integrity/availability of script-process records; no code execution or data exfiltration is demonstrated. Because no VCS metadata is exposed, I could not verify whether the missing annotation is an injected regression or a pre-existing upstream oversight, so confidence is medium. Other plausible leads were reviewed and rejected or left unconfirmed (details below).
